tier_reason: The gist publishes test.c, test.cpp and test.lua plus the compile commands (gcc -O3, g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x) and a 'benchmark' transcript with C 0.234 s, C++ 0.321 s, LuaJIT 0.161 s, but no CPU model, no compiler or LuaJIT versions, and one `time` run per program; the 2020 rerun is a comment with no versions or hardware. First-party numbers with partial methodology, so C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Original 2012 'benchmark' transcript (one `time` run each, real time): C 0.234 s, C++ 0.321 s, Node 0.317 s, LuaJIT 0.161 s, so LuaJIT 1.45x faster than C and 1.99x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Author's 2020-05-26 rerun comment (no versions or hardware): C 0.173 s, C++ 0.36 s, Node 0.5 s, LuaJIT 0.08 s (2.2x vs C, 4.5x vs C++, derived from page data); at 10x iterations LuaJIT 0.76 s, C 1.44 s, C++ 3.35 s (1.9x vs C, 4.4x vs C++, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 test.c; g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x test.cpp; luajit test.lua with default options; no gcc, g++ or LuaJIT versions are given for the 2012 transcript or the 2020 rerun. The gcc 8.3.0, Node v15.12.0 and LuaJIT 2.0.5 named in mbossX's 2021 comment belong to that commenter's own separate 100M-iteration array-based programs (C 0.001 s, LuaJIT 1.774 s), not to the author's numbers.
corrections.workload: Count occurrences of the 19 words of a hard-coded, pre-split sentence over 1,000,000 passes in a string-keyed hash table, one lookup per word per pass. C: hand-written table of 256 buckets indexed by the key's first character, strcmp along each chain, malloc per new counter. C++: std::unordered_map<string,int> over a vector<string> with a custom hash returning s[0], cnt[*it] += 1. Lua: a plain table, `if map[text[i]] then map[text[i]] = map[text[i]] + 1`.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 72 gist stars, 6 forks (2026-10-11); widely cited in LuaJIT vs C discussions
corrections.caveats: The author's a-warning.md (added 2015-08-18) says the benchmark 'has been misleading for a while': hard-coded text, small dictionary, pre-split words, no allocation cost. The author's own 2013 comment in test.lua says 'luajit probably optimizes away all dictionary lookups', which he did not verify. The C and C++ baselines use a first-character hash, so words sharing an initial letter collide and pay full string compares, while Lua strings are interned with a cached hash and compared by pointer; the author notes the default std::hash made C++ 2x slower. Timings are single `time` runs including process startup, with no CPU model and no compiler or LuaJIT versions. Comments show the C++ side can be beaten back: jh3141's fork (2014-12-06, g++ and clang++ -O3) reached 90 ms vs LuaJIT 95 ms and 71 ms with clang++, but it replaced the hash table with a vector of pairs plus a cached next-item pointer and interned pointers, a benchmark-specific structure that does not settle the hash-table comparison either; later array-based C versions (Zack24 2017, mbossX 2021) do no hashing. Source files last changed 2012-07-14 (test.c) and 2013-10-16 (test.lua comment only). No license.
corrections.why_faster: Runtime representation, not code generation: Lua interns every string at creation with a cached hash, so each table lookup is a hash-slot index plus pointer compare, and LuaJIT's trace compiler folds the three map[text[i]] references per iteration into one lookup; test.c walks a first-letter bucket chain with strcmp and test.cpp hashes by first character then compares std::string contents. When C++ was given interned pointers and a benchmark-specific table (jh3141 fork), it matched or beat LuaJIT.

notes: Numbers on the gist match the record (original transcript and the author's 2020 comment); tier C stands as first-party with public code and flags but no CPU or versions. Fixed a misattribution: the gcc 8.3.0 / LuaJIT 2.0.5 versions come from a commenter's separate array-based test, not the author's runs. Shortcomings to record: author-declared misleading benchmark, weak first-letter hash on the C/C++ side versus Lua's interned pre-hashed strings, single-run whole-process timings with no hardware, author's own unverified note that LuaJIT may optimise away the lookups; baseline_stdlib libstdc++ inferred from the g++ toolchain of 2012. Not a reject: the measured work is real on all three sides as far as the source shows.
